title: Tenant transient spill lanes and fragmentation exploration
content:
Summary:
This note explores a complementary layer to our existing KV cache compaction and slab allocator work: a transient spill lane architecture that aims to reduce in-GPU memory fragmentation while preserving tenant isolation guarantees and low tail latency. The idea: instead of immediately compacting or evicting fragmented small entries into a global spill area, route them into per-tenant transient spill lanes (TSLs) with fast write-behind semantics to local NVMe. TSLs are lightweight, time-bounded staging areas for warm-but-dense micro-objects that hurt allocator locality.

Why we need this (motivation):
- Observed: periodic compaction runs cause tail latency spikes and long pauses in high-concurrency workloads (see INF-2143 perf runs).
- Observed: fragmentation in micro-block regions (<256B objects) reduces usable occupancy; compaction is expensive and sometimes unnecessary for short-lived entries.
- Requirement: tenants must remain logically isolated (no cross-tenant eviction poisoning) and quotas enforced.
- Constraint: limited bandwidth to backing NVMe; writes must be amortized and bounded.

Goals:
- Reduce long-running compaction pressure by creating a transient path for micro-objects that are eligible for spill rather than immediate coalescing.
- Preserve tenant-level accounting and quotas while avoiding global synchronization.
- Keep steady-state tail latency within SLOs for hot-path generation requests.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for full compaction/defrag; persistent fragmentation will still require occasional global reclamation.
- Not intended for long-lived cold entries; TSLs are time-bounded (TTL).

High-level design:
1) Per-tenant transient spill lanes (TSLs):
   - Each tenant shard has N lanes (configurable: default 4) mapped to different NVMe queues or logical sub-files to avoid write hotspotting.
   - Lanes accept items based on a small-size threshold (e.g., <= 512 bytes) and a fragmentation score computed at allocation time.
   - Admission decision is local to a shard and requires only local tenant accounting (no global lock).

2) Fast write-behind protocol:
   - Items placed into a TSL are serialized in an append-only segment with a small in-memory index (lane-local).
   - Writes are batched and flushed asynchronously with two durability modes: relaxed (fsync every X batches) and strict (fsync on write) depending on tenant SLA.
   - Each spilled entry keeps a compact tombstone and a recency score so a subsequent request can rehydrate without full NVMe lookup in many cases (see rehydration path).

3) Rehydration and access semantics:
   - On cache miss in main GPU slab, check tenant's TSL index (in CPU memory). If present, schedule an async DMA read to bring item back; optimistic path returns stale-but-acceptable value for some workloads if tenant opts-in.
   - If rehydration is heavy, the scheduler will promote frequently-read TSL objects back into main cache and update allocation heuristics.

4) Eviction integration and fragmentation reduction:
   - Eviction policy for main cache now gains a fourth action: promote->spill->evict->compact. Spill is considered before compaction for small, fragmented items.
   - Each spill reduces allocator pressure and groups small objects into contiguous NVMe segments, lowering fragmentation footprint.

Memory pool model (novel aspects):
- Micro-pools: very small fixed-size pool for sub-512B items with aggressive laneable admission. Micro-pools are mutable: we allow ephemeral overcommit within a lane but track it against tenant soft-quota.
- Thin-pools: mid-size bucket (512B-4KB) where we attempt coalescing instead of immediate spill.
- Backing-pool: large slabs for common allocations (>4KB) unchanged.

Fragmentation scoring (fast heuristic):
- fragmentation_score = (slab_fragmentation_factor * age_weighted_hotness) + occupancy_penalty
- We compute slab_fragmentation_factor by sampling small-run occupancy per micro-pool stripe; if > threshold, items with low recency are TSL-eligible.
- Sampling is probabilistic and uses a tiny reservoir per shard (cheap).

Scheduler integration (latency-aware):
- Introduce a SpillScheduler that accepts spill candidates and limits NVMe inflight IO per-tenant and overall.
- Scheduler priorities: hot-rehydration paths > background batch-fills > periodic lane compaction.
- Backpressure: when NVMe is saturated, fall back to standard eviction (drop) rather than triggering aggressive compaction.

Consistency and correctness model:
- TSL entries are considered lower-tier cache with weaker durability guarantees unless tenant requests strict mode.
- We keep per-tenant monotonic counters to prevent stale rehydrations overshadowing newer updates (lightweight versioning).
- On tenant-level rolling restarts or private deployments, TSL segments can be garbage-collected and reconsumed by compaction if lost.

Operational considerations and observability:
- Metrics to add: TSL_admissions, TSL_hits, TSL_rehydrate_latency_p50/p95/p99, NVMe_write_batch_size, lane_fill_rate, tenant_spill_backpressure_count.
- Traces: attach a TSL span for requests that hit the lane; capture whether rehydration occurred and latency breakdown of NVMe/dma/rehydrate.
- Alerts: NVMe saturation, lane peer imbalance, TSL rehydrate p99 > 50ms.

Testing and experiment plan:
- Local perf sim: extend the existing kv-memory-reclaimer-simulator with a TSL mode; synthetic workloads with micro-object heavy distributions.
- Dogfood: enable for a small set of low-SLA tenants with strict telemetry; compare compaction frequency and overall GPU occupancy.
- A/B: measure p95/p99 generation latency, compaction CPU usage, NVMe bandwidth, and overall cost (tokens/second per GPU).

Rollout and safety knobs:
- Config flags: enable_tsl (per-cluster), tenant_tsl_mode (off/relaxed/strict), lanes_per_shard, max_tsl_bytes_per_tenant, nvme_write_batch_ms.
- Circuit breakers: global NVMe write throttle, lane drain timeout, emergency global compaction if TSLs misbehave.

Open questions / tradeoffs (TODOs to resolve):
- TTL sizing: how long should TSL entries live before forced eviction? 10s/60s/5min? Workload dependent.
- NVMe wear: write-behind will increase writes; need cost model vs compaction CPU/DMA trade.
- Accounting vs fairness: soft-quota overcommit gives better latency but might allow noisy tenants to hoard TSL lanes. Do we introduce per-tenant penalization?
- Rehydration priority: should rehydrate be foreground for some endpoints (e.g., inference) and background for embeddings? Need per-route policy.
- Recovery semantics for Private deployments where customer NVMe may be ephemeral during upgrades.

Implementation sketch (pseudocode snippets):
- TSL admission (simplified):
  if size <= micro_threshold and frag_score >= spill_thresh and tenant_tsl_budget > estimated_spill_cost:
      lane = hash(addr, tenant_id) % lanes_per_shard
      lane.append(batch.serialize(item))
      tenant_tsl_budget -= estimate_cost(item)

- Rehydrate optimistic path:
  if check_lane_index(key):
      submit_async_read(lane.segment_offset)
      if tenant_opt_in_stale && background_read_pending:
        return cached_stale_value
      else
        await read
        promote_to_main_cache()
        return value

Doc posture and style notes:
- This is exploratory; we expect the implementation to iterate. The goal of this doc is to capture ideas that are additive to existing allocator/compaction work without duplicating other proposals.
- Cross-reference: see existing allocator and compaction notes in this folder (search for "compaction" and "micro-slab").

Immediate next steps:
- Spike: build a micro-simulator to model NVMe write cost vs compaction CPU cost for a few synthetic histograms (heavy micro-objects, skewed tenant heatmap). Owner: Arjun. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Prototype: small in-memory lane index + append-only file writer. Owner: Lina. ETA: 4 weeks.
- Telemetry: add TSL metrics and integrate with current trace spans. Owner: Ethan. ETA: 2 weeks.

Notes to self (quick reminders):
- Keep per-tenant data structures compact and lock-free where feasible.
- Avoid cross-tenant compaction coordination; prefer local heuristics.
- Document cost model for NVMe writes and include it in PR description.

References and inspirations:
- INF-2143 perf investigation notes (linked above).
- Prior compaction/allocator docs in this folder; look at cache-slot-coalescer and compact-rewrite heuristics for overlap.
- Academic: write-behind caches and SSD-aware cache eviction papers (TBD list).

Unresolved: add a short decision record once we pick TTL defaults and quota behavior.
